plan.contextChunk: This figure illustrates the architecture of an autoregressive transformer decoder, drawn as a horizontal left-to-right pipeline over a sequence of token positions. At the left, a vertical stack of word-embedding vectors represents the input sequence tokens: <start>, It, takes, great, courage, to, and let. These embeddings enter a large block labeled “Transformer with masked attention,” annotated (× K) to indicate K repeated decoder layers. Inside the transformer block, a lower-triangular masked-attention diagram shows that each token position can attend only to itself and earlier positions, preventing access to future tokens during next-token prediction. The block also shows residual/addition nodes and intermediate feature vectors that pass through the repeated masked-attention layers. At the right, each processed token representation feeds into a “Linear + softmax” block, producing a probability distribution over the vocabulary for the corresponding target token. The target-token labels shown on the far right are It, takes, great, courage, to, let, and yourself, illustrating shifted autoregressive training where the model predicts the next token at each position. This figure introduces the decoder-only transformer architecture for sequence generation, emphasizing causal masking and parallel next-token prediction across positions.

interactions.label: Number of decoder layers K
interactions.teaches: Stacking more decoder layers means the same masked-attention-and-transformation pattern is repeated, letting each token position refine its representation while still obeying the causal mask

Each block has a distinct role in next-token prediction: embeddings turn tokens into vectors, masked attention gathers only past context, residual additions preserve and combine information, and linear plus softmax converts each position into a vocabulary distribution

interactions.label: Trace prediction of 'yourself'
interactions.teaches: The prediction of 'yourself' is produced from the prefix ending in 'let', not from the future target itself, because the causal mask prevents each position from attending to later tokens

demo_steps.title: Shifted next-token targets
demo_steps.narration: The input sequence begins with '<start>' and ends with 'let', while the target labels are shifted one position to the right: '<start>' predicts 'It', 'It' predicts 'takes', and 'let' predicts 'yourself'. This is how the decoder learns next-token prediction in parallel across positions.

demo_steps.title: Causal masked attention
demo_steps.narration: Inside the transformer, the lower-triangular attention pattern shows that each token can attend only to itself and earlier tokens. The row for 'let' may use the whole prefix, but earlier rows cannot look ahead to 'let' or 'yourself'.

demo_steps.title: Repeated decoder layers
demo_steps.narration: Move the K slider to expand or compress the repeated decoder block. Increasing K shows that the same masked-attention structure is stacked multiple times, refining representations without breaking the left-to-right masking rule.

demo_steps.title: Trace the word 'yourself'
demo_steps.narration: Play the trace animation to follow the final input prefix ending at 'let' through embeddings, masked attention, residual additions, and linear plus softmax. The highlighted path ends at the probability row where the target token is 'yourself'.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A decoder transformer can train on all next-token predictions in parallel, but the causal mask makes every prediction behave as if the model only knows the prefix to its left.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the figure as a wide horizontal SVG pipeline. Use a dashed rounded box around the left word embeddings, a larger dashed rounded box around the transformer, orange for the triangular masked-attention matrix, teal for transformation and linear-softmax blocks, blue-gray for feature/probability vectors, and black arrows for data flow. The attention matrix should clearly be lower triangular, with visible diagonal/self-attention and no access to future positions. The K slider should either show a compact '(× K)' notation or expand the central transformer into K stacked miniature masked-attention layers. Clicking a named block should add a bright outline and show a concise tooltip near it. The 'yourself' animation should emphasize the bottom input row corresponding to 'let' and trace its path to the bottom output probability distribution labeled 'yourself'.
